source: J. Groocock, Fugal Composition (ed. Y. Tomita, Greenwood 2003), Appendix A: Episodes, book pp.185-192 (pdf 198-205)
columns_note: The appendix has NO key/modulation or sequence-type columns; only fugue, episode number, bar span and a verbal description of the material. Bracketed (stacked) simultaneous figures are rendered '{a | b}'. Abbreviations: S = subject (Si, Sii, Siii = subject figures 1,2,3), C = countersubject (Ci, Cii = first/second countersubject or countersubject figures), "C" in quotes = quasi-countersubject, Epp. = episodes. Bar ranges are printed abbreviated in places (e.g. '12-3' = 12-13, '107-11' = 107-111); bar_start/bar_end expand them.

appendix_own_claims: Appendix A contains no prose: only the counts table (p.185) and the outline list (pp.186-192).

related_claims_chapter16_Episodes2.claim: In the entire '48' there are well over 200 passages long enough and important enough to rank as episodes.
A fugue may have no episode at all (I.1) or any number from one to nine; II.19 is 29 bars with seven episodes while II.17 is fifty bars long with only two (checked on image).
Episodes can function like a development section, e.g. I.3 bars 28-42, II.11 bar 25-52 (checked on image).

Bach most often develops figures first heard in the exposition (subject/answer, countersubject, free part, codetta); occasionally (notably I.24) completely new material, which is then repeated in later episodes.

Almost all episodes use sequence; the simple falling sequence is commonest, rising far rarer; occasionally repetition a third or fourth higher/lower. Rising sequence harmonized by roots alternately rising a 4th and falling a 3rd; falling by roots falling a 5th / rising a 4th.
At least thirty fugues use interchange in one or more episodes.

In II.19 every one of the seven episodes starts by repeating the final figure of the subject entry in sequence; in I.18 the final subject figure plus accompanying voices is repeated in rising sequence into EP.1 (bar 9) and falling sequence into EP.2 (bar 13).
